question: A 5-year-old child is found pulseless and apnoeic. Two rescuers are present and begin paediatric BLS. Which of the following is the correct compression-to-ventilation ratio and chest compression rate for two-rescuer paediatric CPR?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: 30:2 is the adult (and single-rescuer paediatric) ratio. Two-rescuer paediatric CPR uses 15:2 to allow more ventilations relative to compressions, reflecting the predominantly respiratory aetiology of paediatric arrest.

Correct. Two-rescuer paediatric CPR uses a 15:2 ratio at 100–120 compressions per minute. Compression depth should be approximately one-third of the anterior-posterior chest diameter. This higher ventilation ratio acknowledges that paediatric arrest is almost always secondary to respiratory failure.
The ratio is correct (15:2 for two-rescuer paediatric CPR), but a rate of 60–80/min is too slow. PALS guidelines specify 100–120 compressions per minute to maintain adequate perfusion pressure.
Both elements are incorrect. Two-rescuer paediatric CPR uses 15:2 (not 30:2) and a rate of 100–120/min (not 80–100/min). The 30:2 ratio applies to single-rescuer and adult CPR.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the PALS BLS guidelines. Two-rescuer paediatric CPR uses 15:2 (not 30:2) at 100–120 compressions/min. The one-third AP chest diameter depth rule is unique to paediatrics.

Well done. Two-rescuer paediatric CPR: 15:2 ratio at 100–120 compressions/min, depth one-third AP diameter. Remember: defib is for shockable rhythms (VF/pulseless VT) only — 2–4 J/kg for initial shock.
